ai.uninformed-order.title: BFS and DFS expansion order
ai.uninformed-order.subject: Artificial Intelligence
ai.uninformed-order.check: Write the frontier after every expansion; BFS = FIFO queue, DFS = LIFO/recursion; apply the stated tie rule and skip nodes already seen.

ai.goal-test.title: Goal test on generation vs on expansion
ai.goal-test.subject: Artificial Intelligence
ai.goal-test.check: Test on generation stops while the goal's parent is being expanded; test on expansion lets the goal wait in the frontier (one extra level for BFS). UCS needs the test on expansion.

ai.ucs-trace.title: Uniform-cost search traces
ai.ucs-trace.subject: Artificial Intelligence
ai.ucs-trace.check: Pop the lowest g (ties as stated), lower a frontier node's g when a cheaper path appears, stop only when the goal is popped.

ai.ids.title: Iterative deepening search
ai.ids.subject: Artificial Intelligence
ai.ids.check: Limits 0,1,…,d; each iteration is a fresh DFS from the root. Generated nodes: d·b + (d−1)b² + … + 1·b^d = O(b^d); memory O(bd).

ai.search-props.title: Completeness and optimality of uninformed search
ai.search-props.subject: Artificial Intelligence
ai.search-props.check: BFS/UCS/IDS complete (finite b); DFS not with infinite paths. Optimal: BFS/IDS for unit costs, UCS for costs ≥ ε > 0; DFS never guaranteed.

ai.search-complexity.title: Time and space in b, d, m
ai.search-complexity.subject: Artificial Intelligence
ai.search-complexity.check: BFS time and space O(b^d) (O(b^{d+1}) with late goal test); DFS time O(b^m), space O(bm); IDS O(b^d) time, O(bd) space; UCS O(b^{1+⌊C*/ε⌋}).

questions.stem: Breadth-first search is run on the undirected graph in the figure from start $S$ to goal $G$. Use graph search (a node already in the frontier or already expanded is never added again), generate successors in alphabetical order, and apply the goal test when a node is selected for expansion. In which order are nodes expanded (the goal counts as expanded)?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 315 165" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 79L85 46M35 91L85 124M107 38L158 27M105 46L160 79M105 124L160 91M107 132L158 143M182 27L233 38M182 87L278 108M182 142L278 113M251 50L284 100" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="40" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="130" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="25" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="145" r="12"/><circle cx="245" cy="40" r="12"/><circle cx="290" cy="110" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="89">S</text><text x="95" y="44">A</text><text x="95" y="134">B</text><text x="170" y="29">C</text><text x="170" y="89">D</text><text x="170" y="149">E</text><text x="245" y="44">F</text><text x="290" y="114">G</text></g></svg>

options.text: S, A, C, F, G
options.why: This is the depth-first order: it follows A → C → F → G instead of finishing each level.

options.text: S, A, B, C, D
options.why: Stopped when G was generated (while expanding D); the goal test here is on expansion, so E, F and then G are still dequeued.

options.text: S, A, B, C, D, E, F, G
options.why: FIFO queue: S → (A, B) → A adds C, D → B adds only E (D is already queued) → C adds F → D adds G; E and F are dequeued before G.

options.text: S, A, D, G
options.why: This is the path BFS returns, not the order of expansion; nodes off the path are expanded too.

questions.solution:
1. Queue after S: A, B.
2. A → add C, D. B → D already queued, add E.
3. C → add F. D → add G. E → G already queued.
4. F, then G is dequeued and passes the goal test: S, A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

questions.stem: Recursive depth-first search is run on the graph in the figure from $S$ to goal $G$. Unvisited neighbours are tried in alphabetical order, a node is never visited twice, and the search stops as soon as $G$ is visited. Which visiting order results?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 315 165" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 79L85 46M35 91L85 124M107 38L158 27M105 46L160 79M105 124L160 91M107 132L158 143M182 27L233 38M182 87L278 108M182 142L278 113M251 50L284 100" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="40" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="130" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="25" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="145" r="12"/><circle cx="245" cy="40" r="12"/><circle cx="290" cy="110" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="89">S</text><text x="95" y="44">A</text><text x="95" y="134">B</text><text x="170" y="29">C</text><text x="170" y="89">D</text><text x="170" y="149">E</text><text x="245" y="44">F</text><text x="290" y="114">G</text></g></svg>

options.text: S, A, B, C, D, E, F, G
options.why: That is the breadth-first (level-by-level) order; DFS goes deep along the first branch.

options.text: S, A, D, G
options.why: That is the shortest path; DFS from A tries C before D, so it reaches G through C and F.

options.text: S, A, C, F, G
options.why: S → A (first alphabetically) → C (first unvisited neighbour of A) → F → G, which is the goal.

options.text: S, B, E, G
options.why: Tried neighbours in reverse alphabetical order (B before A), like pushing children onto a stack in the wrong order.

questions.solution:
1. S → A (A < B).
2. A's unvisited neighbours: C, D → go to C.
3. C → F → G (goal). Order S, A, C, F, G; the path found has 4 edges, not the shortest.

questions.stem: In the tree shown, children are generated left to right and the goal test is applied when a node is expanded (the goal counts as expanded). The goal is $J$. Let $n_B$ and $n_D$ be the numbers of nodes expanded by BFS and by DFS. What is $n_B-n_D$?

traps.why: Reported $n_B$ alone; the question asks for the difference.
Subtracted in the wrong order ($n_D-n_B$).
Did not count the goal $J$ as expanded in one of the two searches.
Counted BFS one node past the goal; BFS stops exactly at $J$, the 10th node in level order.

questions.solution:
1. BFS (level order): A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J → $n_B=10$.
2. DFS: A, B, D, H, I, E, J → $n_D=7$.
3. $n_B-n_D=3$.

questions.stem: In the tree shown, the goal is $G$. Children are generated left to right and the goal test is applied on expansion (the goal counts as expanded). Which statements are correct?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 158" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M154 20L66 54M167 27L174 47M174 20L248 54M48 66L23 92M64 66L88 92M177 69L177 89M252 67L237 91M264 67L279 91M15 111L15 131M90 109L75 133M102 109L117 133M177 111L177 131M231 111L231 131" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="15" cy="142" r="11"/><circle cx="15" cy="100" r="11"/><circle cx="69" cy="142" r="11"/><circle cx="123" cy="142" r="11"/><circle cx="96" cy="100" r="11"/><circle cx="56" cy="58" r="11"/><circle cx="177" cy="142" r="11"/><circle cx="177" cy="100" r="11"/><circle cx="177" cy="58" r="11"/><circle cx="231" cy="142" r="11"/><circle cx="231" cy="100" r="11"/><circle cx="285" cy="100" r="11"/><circle cx="258" cy="58" r="11"/><circle cx="164" cy="16" r="11"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="15" y="146">J</text><text x="15" y="104">E</text><text x="69" y="146">K</text><text x="123" y="146">L</text><text x="96" y="104">F</text><text x="56" y="62">B</text><text x="177" y="146">M</text><text x="177" y="104">G</text><text x="177" y="62">C</text><text x="231" y="146">N</text><text x="231" y="104">H</text><text x="285" y="104">I</text><text x="258" y="62">D</text><text x="164" y="20">A</text></g></svg>

options.text: BFS expands 7 nodes.
options.why: Level order A, B, C, D, E, F, G: the goal is the 7th node dequeued.

options.text: DFS expands fewer nodes than BFS.
options.why: DFS first exhausts B's whole subtree (E, J, F, K, L) before reaching C, so it expands 9 nodes; DFS is not always cheaper.

options.text: DFS expands 9 nodes.
options.why: A, B, E, J, F, K, L, C, G: nine expansions.

options.text: DFS returns a longer path to $G$ than BFS.
options.why: In a tree each node has exactly one path from the root, so both return A–C–G.

questions.solution:
1. BFS: A, B, C, D, E, F, G → 7.
2. DFS: A, B, E, J, F, K, L, C, G → 9.
3. Paths in a tree are unique, so both return A → C → G.

questions.stem: Recursive depth-first graph search runs on the **directed** graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$. Successors are tried in alphabetical order, visited nodes are skipped, and the search stops when $G$ is visited. Which path does DFS return?

options.text: S → A → B → S → C → D → G
options.why: Followed the edge B → S back to the visited start; graph search skips visited nodes, so no cycle enters the path.

options.text: S → C → D → G
options.why: Tried C before A; alphabetical order puts A first at S.

options.text: S → A → E → G
options.why: That is the fewest-edge path BFS would return; DFS commits to A's first successor B before trying E.

options.text: S → A → B → D → G
options.why: From S go to A, from A to B (B < E); B's successor S is visited, so go to D, then G.

questions.solution:
1. S → A (A < C).
2. A → B (B < E).
3. B: S already visited, so → D.
4. D → G. Path S, A, B, D, G (4 edges), while BFS would find S, A, E, G (3 edges).

questions.stem: Breadth-first graph search runs on the **directed** graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$. Successors are generated alphabetically, a node already in the frontier or already expanded is not added again, and the goal test is applied on expansion. In which order are nodes expanded?

options.text: S, A, B, D, G
options.why: That is the depth-first order; BFS finishes A's sibling C before going deeper.

options.text: S, A, C, B, E, D, S, G
options.why: Re-added S through the edge B → S; graph search never re-adds an expanded node.

options.text: S, A, C, B, E, D, G
options.why: Queue: S → A, C → (A adds B, E) → C adds D → B adds nothing new (S expanded, D queued) → E adds G → D → G.

options.text: S, A, C, B, E
options.why: Stopped when G was generated while expanding E; with the test on expansion, D and then G are still dequeued.

questions.solution:
1. Expand S: queue A, C.
2. A: add B, E. C: add D.
3. B: S expanded, D queued → nothing. E: add G.
4. D: G queued → nothing. Dequeue G. Order S, A, C, B, E, D, G.

questions.stem: Breadth-first graph search is run on the undirected graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$, generating successors alphabetically. This time the goal test is applied **when a node is generated**, and the search stops at that moment. How many nodes are expanded (have their successors generated)?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 315 165" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 79L85 46M35 91L85 124M107 38L158 27M105 46L160 79M105 124L160 91M107 132L158 143M182 27L233 38M182 87L278 108M182 142L278 113M251 50L284 100" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="40" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="130" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="25" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="145" r="12"/><circle cx="245" cy="40" r="12"/><circle cx="290" cy="110" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="89">S</text><text x="95" y="44">A</text><text x="95" y="134">B</text><text x="170" y="29">C</text><text x="170" y="89">D</text><text x="170" y="149">E</text><text x="245" y="44">F</text><text x="290" y="114">G</text></g></svg>

traps.why: Applied the goal test on expansion instead: then E, F and G are also dequeued.
Counted G as expanded; with the test on generation G is detected while D is being expanded and is never expanded.
Stopped before expanding D, but G is only generated when D (the first node adjacent to G in the queue) is expanded.

questions.solution:
1. Expand S (gen A, B), A (gen C, D), B (gen E), C (gen F).
2. Expand D: generates G, which passes the goal test.
3. Expanded: S, A, B, C, D → 5.

questions.stem: Breadth-first search on a tree with branching factor $b$ and shallowest goal at depth $d$ is changed so that the goal test is done **when a node is expanded** instead of when it is generated. In the worst case, the number of nodes generated becomes

options.text: $O(b^d)$, unchanged
options.why: With a test on expansion the goal waits in the queue while every other depth-$d$ node is expanded and generates its children.

options.text: $O(bd)$
options.why: That is the memory of DFS or IDS, not the node count of BFS.
Each depth-$d$ node before the goal is expanded, so nearly a full extra level of $b^{d+1}$ children is generated.
Squared the bound; delaying the test adds only one level, a factor of $b$.

questions.solution:
1. Test on generation: stop when the goal is created → $b+b^2+\dots+b^d=O(b^d)$.
2. Test on expansion: all depth-$d$ nodes ahead of the goal are expanded → adds up to $b^{d+1}$ nodes.
3. So $O(b^{d+1})$.

questions.stem: BFS runs on a complete binary tree (branching factor 2). The only goal is the **last** node at depth 3 in left-to-right order. The goal test is applied **when a node is expanded**, and expanding a node generates both its children. Counting the root, how many nodes are generated in total when the search stops?

traps.why: Used the goal test on generation: the search would stop as soon as the goal is created ($1+2+4+8$).
Also expanded the goal itself; the search stops when the goal is selected, before its children are generated.
Reported only the extra nodes caused by the late test ($7\times 2$), not the total generated.

questions.solution:
1. Before the goal is dequeued, all of depths 0–3 have been generated: $1+2+4+8=15$.
2. The 7 depth-3 nodes ahead of the goal are expanded, adding $7\times 2=14$ nodes.
3. Total $15+14=29$.

questions.stem: For which strategy does applying the goal test at generation time (instead of at expansion) break its optimality guarantee?

options.text: Uniform-cost search
options.why: A goal generated early may carry a high $g$; a cheaper path can still be found later, so UCS must wait until the goal is popped.

options.text: Iterative deepening search with unit step costs
options.why: Each IDS iteration finds the shallowest goal either way; the test position changes cost, not optimality.

options.text: Depth-first search
options.why: DFS is not optimal under either rule, so there is no guarantee to break.

options.text: Breadth-first search with unit step costs
options.why: For BFS the first goal generated is already at the shallowest depth, so an early test keeps it optimal and saves work.

questions.solution:
1. BFS/IDS: optimal for unit costs; an early test is safe.
2. UCS: optimality comes from popping in increasing $g$; testing on generation can return a costlier path.

questions.stem: Uniform-cost search runs on the weighted graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$ (ties broken alphabetically). Which statements are correct?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 170" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 78L100 37M35 92L100 133M120 37L180 78M120 133L180 92M202 82L283 63M122 32L283 58M122 141L218 149M237 140L288 70" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="110" cy="30" r="12"/><circle cx="110" cy="140" r="12"/><circle cx="190" cy="85" r="12"/><circle cx="230" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="295" cy="60" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="89">S</text><text x="110" y="34">A</text><text x="110" y="144">B</text><text x="190" y="89">C</text><text x="230" y="154">D</text><text x="295" y="64">G</text><text x="72" y="69">2</text><text x="63" y="124">2</text><text x="145" y="69">2</text><text x="145" y="109">1</text><text x="245" y="85">3</text><text x="201" y="58">6</text><text x="169" y="158">3</text><text x="255" y="104">2</text></g></svg>

options.text: With the goal test on generation, the search stops after expanding S and A and returns a path of cost 8.
options.why: A is popped first (tie with B, alphabetical) and generates G with $g=2+6=8$; the early test accepts it.

options.text: With the goal test on expansion, the returned path costs 6.
options.why: G is popped with $g=6$ via S–B–C–G, after C (3) and D (5).

options.text: Both placements return the same path because UCS orders the frontier by cost.
options.why: Ordering helps only if the goal must be popped; a generation-time test accepts the first, costly copy of G.

options.text: With the goal test on expansion, the returned path is S–A–C–G.
options.why: S–A–C–G costs 7; C is reached more cheaply via B (cost 3), so the parent of C is B.

questions.solution:
1. Pop S: A=2, B=2. Pop A (tie, alphabetical): C=4, G=8 ← early test stops here (cost 8).
2. Otherwise pop B: C→3, D=5. Pop C: G→6. Pop D: G stays 6.
3. Pop G at 6 via S–B–C–G.

questions.stem: Uniform-cost graph search runs on the weighted undirected graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$. A frontier node's cost is lowered if a cheaper path is found, ties are broken alphabetically, and the goal test is done when a node is popped. In what order are nodes expanded (the goal counts)?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 325 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 29L100 73M28 34L57 138M103 90L67 140M122 83L178 97M71 146L179 104M72 151L238 159M198 108L242 152M200 93L290 29M254 149L296 33M37 22L288 22" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="22" r="12"/><circle cx="110" cy="80" r="12"/><circle cx="60" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="190" cy="100" r="12"/><circle cx="250" cy="160" r="12"/><circle cx="300" cy="22" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="26">S</text><text x="110" y="84">A</text><text x="60" y="154">B</text><text x="190" y="104">C</text><text x="250" y="164">D</text><text x="300" y="26">G</text><text x="62" y="62">1</text><text x="34" y="92">4</text><text x="78" y="114">2</text><text x="148" y="103">5</text><text x="128" y="137">1</text><text x="155" y="168">5</text><text x="214" y="140">2</text><text x="250" y="72">6</text><text x="283" y="98">2</text><text x="162" y="35">12</text></g></svg>

options.text: S, A, B, C, G
options.why: Popped G after C at cost 10, but D (cost 6) and the path through D (cost 8) are cheaper.

options.text: S, A, B, C, D, G
options.why: Pop costs: S 0, A 1, B 3 (via A), C 4 (via B), D 6 (via C), G 8 (via D).

options.text: S, G
options.why: Stopped when G was generated from S with cost 12; UCS waits until G is popped, and cheaper paths still exist.

options.text: S, A, C, B, D, G
options.why: Treated A–C (cost 5) as cheaper than reaching B via A (1+2=3); UCS orders by total path cost $g$, not single edge weights.

questions.solution:
1. Expand S: A=1, B=4, G=12.
2. A: B→3, C=6. B: C→4, D=8.
3. C: D→6, G→10. D: G→8.
4. Pop G at 8. Order S, A, B, C, D, G.

questions.stem: For the graph in the figure, what is the cost of the path returned by uniform-cost search from $S$ to $G$ (goal test when popped)?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 325 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 29L100 73M28 34L57 138M103 90L67 140M122 83L178 97M71 146L179 104M72 151L238 159M198 108L242 152M200 93L290 29M254 149L296 33M37 22L288 22" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="22" r="12"/><circle cx="110" cy="80" r="12"/><circle cx="60" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="190" cy="100" r="12"/><circle cx="250" cy="160" r="12"/><circle cx="300" cy="22" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="26">S</text><text x="110" y="84">A</text><text x="60" y="154">B</text><text x="190" y="104">C</text><text x="250" y="164">D</text><text x="300" y="26">G</text><text x="62" y="62">1</text><text x="34" y="92">4</text><text x="78" y="114">2</text><text x="148" y="103">5</text><text x="128" y="137">1</text><text x="155" y="168">5</text><text x="214" y="140">2</text><text x="250" y="72">6</text><text x="283" y="98">2</text><text x="162" y="35">12</text></g></svg>

traps.why: Returned the direct edge S–G: that is what BFS (fewest edges) or a goal test on generation gives.
Took G when it was first improved via C (4+6), or went A → C directly (1+5+2+2); D at cost 6 is popped first and lowers G to 8.
Used S–B–D–G with the edge S–B (4), missing that B is cheaper via A (3) and that C–D is a shortcut.

questions.solution:
1. Cheapest costs: A=1, B=3, C=4, D=6.
2. G via D: 6+2=8, via C: 10, direct: 12.
3. Path S–A–B–C–D–G, cost 8.

questions.stem: On the graph in the figure (search from $S$ to $G$), which statements are correct?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 325 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 29L100 73M28 34L57 138M103 90L67 140M122 83L178 97M71 146L179 104M72 151L238 159M198 108L242 152M200 93L290 29M254 149L296 33M37 22L288 22" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="22" r="12"/><circle cx="110" cy="80" r="12"/><circle cx="60" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="190" cy="100" r="12"/><circle cx="250" cy="160" r="12"/><circle cx="300" cy="22" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="26">S</text><text x="110" y="84">A</text><text x="60" y="154">B</text><text x="190" y="104">C</text><text x="250" y="164">D</text><text x="300" y="26">G</text><text x="62" y="62">1</text><text x="34" y="92">4</text><text x="78" y="114">2</text><text x="148" y="103">5</text><text x="128" y="137">1</text><text x="155" y="168">5</text><text x="214" y="140">2</text><text x="250" y="72">6</text><text x="283" y="98">2</text><text x="162" y="35">12</text></g></svg>

options.text: BFS (fewest edges) returns a path of cost 12.
options.why: S–G is a single edge, so BFS returns it, ignoring its cost.

options.text: UCS with the goal test on expansion returns a path of cost 8.
options.why: G is popped only when its cost is 8, via S–A–B–C–D–G.

options.text: UCS with the goal test on generation also returns cost 8.
options.why: G is generated while expanding S, with cost 12, so the search would stop immediately.

options.text: UCS expands D before C.
options.why: C is popped at cost 4, D at 6; $g$ order puts C first.

questions.solution:
1. BFS: S → G directly (cost 12).
2. UCS (test on pop): costs A 1, B 3, C 4, D 6, G 8.
3. Testing on generation stops at the cost-12 copy of G.

questions.stem: Uniform-cost search (goal test on pop, frontier costs lowered when a cheaper path is found) runs from $S$ to $G$ on the undirected graph with edges S–A (3), S–B (1), B–A (1), A–G (2), B–C (4), C–G (1). What is $g(A)$ at the moment $A$ is expanded?

traps.why: Kept the first cost found for A (direct edge from S); B is popped first at cost 1 and lowers A to 1+1=2.
Used the single edge weight B–A instead of the total path cost from S.
Gave the cost of the goal G (2+2), not of A.

questions.solution:
1. Pop S: A=3, B=1.
2. Pop B (1): A lowered to 2, C=5.
3. Pop A with $g(A)=2$ (then G=4 is popped next).

questions.stem: Uniform-cost search runs on the graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$; ties are broken alphabetically, the goal test is applied when a node is popped, and frontier costs are lowered when a cheaper path appears. In which order are nodes expanded?

options.text: S, A, C, G
options.why: Followed A's cheapest edges like a depth-first walk; UCS keeps every frontier node and always pops the global minimum $g$.

options.text: S, A, B, C, G
options.why: Skipped D: after C is popped at 3, D ($g=5$) is cheaper than G ($g=6$) and is popped first.

options.text: S, A, B, C, D, G
options.why: Pops at g = 0, 2, 2, 3 (C via B), 5 (D), 6 (G via C).

options.text: S, B, A, C, D, G
options.why: Broke the tie between A and B (both $g=2$) the wrong way; alphabetical order pops A first.

questions.solution:
1. S: A=2, B=2.
2. A (tie → alphabetical): C=4, G=8. B: C→3, D=5.
3. C (3): G→6. D (5): G stays 6.
4. G popped at 6.

questions.stem: Iterative deepening search runs depth limits $0,1,2,\dots$ on a complete tree with branching factor 2. The only goal is the **last** node at depth 3 (in left-to-right order), so every iteration runs to completion. Counting each visit of a node in every iteration (the root counts each time), how many node visits are made in total?

traps.why: Counted only the final iteration (limit 3): $1+2+4+8$.
Left out the final iteration that actually finds the goal ($1+3+7$).
Counted only the nodes below the root in the final iteration ($2+4+8$).

questions.stem: Iterative deepening search starts with depth limit 0 and raises the limit by 1 each time. The shallowest goal is at depth 4. How many times is the root node visited in total?

traps.why: Started the count at limit 1 or stopped at limit 3; limits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 give five iterations.
Treated IDS like a single DFS; every iteration restarts from the root.

questions.solution:
1. Iterations use limits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
2. Each starts at the root → 5 visits.

questions.stem: Iterative deepening search (limits $0,1,2,\dots$; children left to right; goal test on visit) runs on the tree shown with goal $F$. What is the complete sequence of node visits?

options.text: A, B, C, D, E, F
options.why: That is the BFS order; IDS revisits the upper levels in every iteration.

options.text: A, B, D, E, C, F
options.why: That is a single depth-first pass; IDS first runs the shallower limits 0 and 1.

options.text: A, A, B, C, A, B, D, E, C, F
options.why: Limit 0: A. Limit 1: A, B, C. Limit 2: A, B, D, E, C, F (goal).

options.text: A, A, B, C, A, B, C, D, E, F
options.why: Visited depth 1 completely before depth 2 within the last iteration; each iteration is depth-first, so D, E come right after B.

questions.solution:
1. Limit 0: A.
2. Limit 1: A, B, C.
3. Limit 2: A, B, D, E, C, F → stop at F.

questions.stem: In the worst case, iterative deepening search with branching factor $b=3$ and shallowest goal depth $d=4$ generates $N=d\,b+(d-1)\,b^2+\dots+1\cdot b^d$ nodes (the root is not counted). What is $N$?

traps.why: Used the BFS count $b+b^2+b^3+b^4$, which generates each level once.
Counted only the deepest level $b^d$.
Added the root once per iteration (5 iterations); the formula excludes the root.
Reversed the multipliers ($1\cdot b+2b^2+3b^3+4b^4$); the deepest level is generated only once and the shallowest $d$ times.

questions.stem: Which statements about iterative deepening search (IDS) with finite branching factor $b$ and shallowest goal depth $d$ are correct?

options.text: Although shallow nodes are regenerated many times, total time is still $O(b^d)$.
options.why: Most nodes are on the deepest level, which is generated only once; the repeats add a constant factor about $b/(b-1)$.

options.text: IDS needs $O(b^d)$ memory, like BFS.
options.why: Swapped with BFS; each iteration is depth-first and stores one path with its siblings, $O(bd)$.

options.text: IDS returns a goal at the same depth as plain DFS would.
options.why: Plain DFS may return a deeper goal on its leftmost branch; IDS raises the limit one level at a time, so it returns a shallowest goal, like BFS.

options.text: IDS remains complete even if $b$ is infinite.
options.why: With infinite $b$ even the limit-1 iteration never finishes; completeness needs finite $b$.

questions.solution:
1. Time $O(b^d)$, memory $O(bd)$.
2. Finds a shallowest goal (optimal for unit costs).
3. Completeness needs finite $b$.

questions.stem: A state space has finite branching factor $b$, every action costs 1, and the shallowest goal is at depth $d$, but some paths are infinitely long. Which strategy is guaranteed to be both complete and optimal?

options.text: Breadth-first search
options.why: BFS finishes each depth before the next, so it reaches depth $d$ in finite time and the first goal found is a shallowest one, which is optimal for unit costs.

options.text: Depth-first search
options.why: DFS can run forever down an infinite path, so it is not complete here, and it need not find the shallowest goal.

options.text: Greedy best-first search
options.why: Greedy ignores path cost (it orders by $h$ only), so it is not optimal even with unit costs.

options.text: Depth-limited search with limit $\ell=d-1$
options.why: A limit below $d$ cuts off every goal, so this search can never succeed.

questions.solution:
1. Unit costs ⇒ shallowest goal = cheapest goal.
2. BFS explores level by level, so it is complete (finite $b$) and returns the shallowest goal.
3. DFS is incomplete with infinite paths; greedy ignores $g$.

questions.stem: Which statements about depth-first search are correct?

options.text: It always returns the shallowest goal.
options.why: DFS returns the first goal on its leftmost descent, which may be deeper than another goal.

options.text: Tree-search DFS can loop forever on a finite graph that has a cycle.
options.why: Without a visited set DFS can walk round the cycle again and again, so it is incomplete there.

options.text: Graph-search DFS (with a visited set) is complete on a finite graph.
options.why: Each node is visited at most once, so the search ends after finitely many steps and finds a reachable goal.

options.text: DFS is optimal whenever all step costs are equal.
options.why: Equal costs make the shallowest goal the cheapest, but DFS does not return the shallowest goal.

questions.solution:
1. DFS is never optimal in general.
2. Tree search can cycle; graph search on a finite graph terminates and is complete.

questions.stem: Which statements about uniform-cost search (UCS) are correct?

options.text: If every step cost is at least some $\varepsilon>0$, UCS is complete and optimal.
options.why: Costs bounded away from 0 mean $g$ grows along every path, so the goal is popped in finite time, and popping in order of $g$ makes the first goal popped the cheapest.

options.text: UCS remains optimal when some edges have negative cost.
options.why: A negative edge found later can make an already-popped path cheaper; UCS assumes costs are non-negative.

options.text: With all step costs equal, UCS expands nodes in non-decreasing order of depth, like BFS.
options.why: $g$ is then a constant times depth, so ordering by $g$ is ordering by depth.

options.text: UCS stops as soon as the goal is generated, which is what makes it optimal.
options.why: That reverses the rule: UCS must wait until the goal is popped; a goal generated early may be reached later by a cheaper path.

questions.solution:
1. Optimality needs costs ≥ ε > 0 and the goal test on expansion.
2. Negative costs break the 'popped = final' property.
3. Equal costs: $g\propto$ depth, so UCS behaves like BFS.

questions.stem: Which statement about iterative deepening search (IDS) with branching factor $b$ and shallowest goal depth $d$ is correct?

options.text: It is optimal for any positive step costs.
options.why: IDS finds the shallowest goal; that is cheapest only when all step costs are equal.

options.text: It is complete, optimal for unit step costs, uses $O(bd)$ memory and $O(b^d)$ time.
options.why: IDS combines BFS's level-by-level guarantee with DFS's linear memory.

options.text: Its memory is $O(b^d)$, the same as BFS.
options.why: Swapped with BFS; each IDS iteration is a depth-first search, which stores only one path with siblings.

options.text: Re-expanding shallow levels makes its time $O(b^{d+1})$.
options.why: The repeated levels are small: level $i$ is redone $d-i+1$ times, and the total stays $O(b^d)$.

questions.solution:
1. Each iteration is DFS with limit $\ell$ → memory $O(bd)$.
2. Total generated $= db+(d-1)b^2+\dots+1\cdot b^d=O(b^d)$.
3. Finds the shallowest goal → optimal only for unit costs.

questions.stem: Step costs in a problem are positive but unequal. Which uninformed strategy is guaranteed to return a cheapest path?

options.text: Uniform-cost search
options.why: UCS expands in increasing path cost $g$ and tests the goal when popped, so the first goal popped is a cheapest one (costs ≥ ε > 0).

options.text: Iterative deepening search
options.why: IDS also returns the shallowest goal, so it has the same unit-cost restriction as BFS.

options.text: Depth-first search
options.why: DFS ignores both depth and cost when choosing a branch; it returns the first goal on its leftmost path.

options.text: Breadth-first search
options.why: BFS returns the path with the fewest edges, which is cheapest only when all step costs are equal.

questions.solution:
1. Unequal costs: fewest edges ≠ cheapest.
2. UCS orders by $g$ and is optimal for costs ≥ ε > 0.

questions.stem: BFS with the goal test on generation runs on a tree with branching factor $b=3$. In the worst case the goal is the last node at depth $d=4$. Not counting the root, how many nodes are generated?

traps.why: Counted the root, which the question excludes.
Counted only the deepest level $b^d$.
Added a further level ($3^5=243$) as if the goal test were on expansion.
Used the iterative deepening count $db+(d-1)b^2+\dots$.

questions.stem: Depth-first tree search keeps in memory the root and, for each node on the current path, all $b$ children generated when it was expanded (subtrees already explored are discarded). With $b=4$ and maximum depth $m=5$, what is the largest number of nodes stored at any time?

traps.why: Used $b^m$, the BFS-style level size; DFS keeps only one branch's siblings per level.
Forgot the root ($bm$ only).
Stored only the current path ($m+1$ nodes) and none of the unexpanded siblings.

questions.solution:
1. At depth 5 the path has 5 expanded ancestors (depths 0–4), each with 4 stored children.
2. Storage $=1+bm=1+4\cdot 5=21$, i.e. $O(bm)$.

questions.stem: With $b=10$ and goal depth $d=5$, worst-case BFS (goal test on generation) generates $b+b^2+\dots+b^5$ nodes and IDS generates $5b+4b^2+3b^3+2b^4+b^5$. About how many more nodes does IDS generate than BFS?

options.text: About 5 times as many
options.why: Assumed every level is regenerated $d$ times; only the shallow, small levels are repeated often.

options.text: About twice as many
options.why: Doubling would happen for $b=2$ (ratio about $b/(b-1)$); for $b=10$ the overhead is near $10/9$.

options.text: Exactly the same number
options.why: IDS does regenerate shallow levels; the overhead is small but not zero.

options.text: About 11% more

questions.stem: With branching factor $b$, shallowest goal depth $d$, maximum depth $m$, optimal cost $C^*$ and minimum step cost $\varepsilon$, which complexity statements are correct?

options.text: BFS time is $O(b^d)$ (goal test on generation).
options.why: It generates every level up to $d$, dominated by $b^d$.

options.text: DFS space is $O(b^m)$.
options.why: Swapped time and space: DFS time is $O(b^m)$ but it stores only $O(bm)$ nodes.

options.text: UCS time is $O(b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\varepsilon\rfloor})$.
options.why: UCS explores every node with $g<C^*$; such paths have at most $\lfloor C^*/\varepsilon\rfloor$ steps, plus one level of generation.

options.text: BFS space is $O(b^d)$.
options.why: BFS keeps the whole frontier, which holds a full level of about $b^d$ nodes.

questions.solution:
1. BFS: time and space $O(b^d)$.
2. DFS: time $O(b^m)$, space $O(bm)$.
3. IDS: time $O(b^d)$, space $O(bd)$.
4. UCS: $O(b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\varepsilon\rfloor})$.

questions.stem: BFS must keep about $b^d$ nodes in memory. With $b=10$, goal depth $d=6$ and 1 KB per node, roughly how much memory is needed, and how much would IDS need?

options.text: About 1 MB for BFS; about 60 KB for IDS
options.why: Used $10^3$ nodes (depth 3) for BFS; $b^d=10^6$.

options.text: About 1 TB for BFS; about 1 GB for IDS
options.why: Multiplied by an extra $10^3$ and gave IDS exponential memory; IDS memory is linear in $d$.

options.text: About 1 GB for both
options.why: Gave IDS the BFS memory; IDS keeps only one path with its siblings, $O(bd)$.

options.text: About 1 GB for BFS; about 60 KB for IDS
options.why: $10^6$ nodes × 1 KB ≈ 1 GB; IDS stores about $bd=60$ nodes ≈ 60 KB.

questions.solution:
1. BFS: $b^d=10^6$ nodes × 1 KB ≈ 1 GB.
2. IDS: $bd=60$ nodes × 1 KB ≈ 60 KB.
